draft.title: Associations between categorical variables
card: A two-way table shows counts for two categorical variables at once. One variable runs down the rows and the other across the columns.
Raw counts can mislead when the groups differ in size. So turn the counts into percentages of each column total, or each row total, as set by the explanatory variable.

Percentages are taken within each group of the explanatory variable. Then compare them across the groups. Example: 30 of 60 Year 11 students walk to school (50%), and 20 of 80 Year 12 students do (25%).
If the percentages differ clearly between the groups, there is an association. If they are about the same, there is no association. In the example, walking is associated with year level.
draft.remember: Find percentages within each explanatory group, then compare them. Different percentages mean an association.

a.q: In a survey, 40 of 80 members of Club A and 30 of 60 members of Club B prefer swimming. What does this show about club and preference?
opts: No association, as 50% in both clubs prefer swimming
An association, as Club A has more swimmers than Club B
An association, as Club A has a larger total than Club B
No association, as both clubs have the same total count
a.why: Club A: 40 ÷ 80 = 50%. Club B: 30 ÷ 60 = 50%. The percentages are the same, so there is no association. Comparing the counts (40 and 30) is tempting, but the clubs differ in size, so counts mislead.
a.clue: Turn each count into a percentage of its own club.

b.q: In a school, 54 of 90 Year 9 students and 36 of 120 Year 10 students own a bike. Which statement is correct?
opts: Bike ownership is associated with year level, 60% to 30%
Bike ownership is associated with year level, 54% to 36%
Bike ownership is not associated with year level, as 90 > 36
Bike ownership is not associated with year level, as 54 > 36
b.why: Year 9: 54 ÷ 90 = 60%. Year 10: 36 ÷ 120 = 30%. The percentages differ clearly, so there is an association. The counts 54 and 36 are not percentages, so using them as percentages is a mistake.
b.clue: Divide each count by its own year total, not by the overall total.

a.best: No association, as 50% in both clubs prefer swimming

b.best: Bike ownership is associated with year level, 60% to 30%

problems.detail: The remember line says 'Different percentages mean an association', but the card says the percentages must 'differ clearly'. Dropping 'clearly' suggests any small difference shows an association.

The right option is the only one that gives a percentage (50%), while all the distractors cite counts or totals. Since the card stresses percentages, a student could pick it without doing the calculation.

check.summary: The facts and answers are correct. The remember line drops the card's 'clearly', so it implies any difference in percentages shows an association. In question a, the right option is the only one giving a percentage, so it stands out.
